does: Scatters flour over food that is already cooking in fat and cooks it for a moment, so that the liquid added next thickens as it simmers.

intro.what: This method scatters flour over food already cooking in fat before adding liquid.
intro.why: It teaches another route to thickening a sauce, with attention to even coating and cooking the flour first.

how: Scatter the flour evenly over the hot, fat-coated food, not in a heap.
Cook it for a moment, stirring, to take away the raw taste.
Add the liquid little by little at first, stirring it smooth.

cues.text: The flour vanishes into a thin paste that coats every piece.
The raw, dusty smell gives way to a faint smell of biscuit.

mistakes.mistake: Tipping the flour in as a heap, which makes lumps that never dissolve.
mistakes.fix: Scatter it from high up, or through a sieve.

mistakes.mistake: Adding the liquid at once, before the flour has cooked.
mistakes.fix: Give it a moment on the heat first.

quiz.question: What is the flour meant to do when liquid is added?
choices: Thicken the liquid as it simmers.
Keep the cooking fat separate from the sauce.
quiz.because: Flour cooked on the fat-coated food thickens the liquid added next.

quiz.question: How should the flour meet the food?
choices: As a heap left on top.
In a heap stirred in after all the liquid has been added.
Scattered evenly over hot food already coated in fat.
quiz.because: Scattering flour evenly coats the food without leaving heaps that can form lumps.

quiz.question: What appearance should follow stirring in the flour?
choices: A thin paste coating the pieces, with no white flour showing.
Loose white heaps between the pieces.
Dry flour floating on liquid added immediately.
quiz.because: No loose white flour should remain visible: it forms a thin paste coating the pieces.

quiz.question: A heap of flour has formed lumps. What would help prevent this next time?
choices: Add the flour all at once and rely on stirring to break it up.
Scatter the flour evenly or use a sieve.
Add all the liquid before stirring the flour.
quiz.because: Scattering flour or using a sieve avoids heaps that turn into lumps.

variant_of.differs: The flour goes onto food already cooking in fat, so that the roux forms around the pieces and is not made on its own.
